opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a natural question, and honestly I don't see them purely as competitors. A lot of this comes from where we started. Our roots are in open-source inference. The engine work came out of research, and from the beginning the goal was to make serving large models faster and cheaper for everyone, not just for one platform.

Companies like Baseten and Fireworks are doing very valuable work. They've built strong businesses around hosted inference: taking models, putting them behind an API, and handling the operations, scaling, and reliability for customers. That's a real need, and they execute well on it. Some of these platforms, or teams like them, actually use or build on open-source engines, so in some sense we're part of the same ecosystem. When the underlying engine gets better, everyone serving models benefits.

Where we focus is a bit different. We care most about the infrastructure layer itself: the runtime, the scheduling, the caching, how you get the most out of the hardware, and how you support new model architectures and new workloads like agents, long context, and reinforcement learning rollouts as quickly as possible. A lot of the large companies and frontier labs we talk to don't want to hand their whole inference stack to a third-party API. They want to run it themselves, on their own clusters, with full control. For them, a strong open-source foundation plus deep engineering support is exactly what they need.

So I'd say there's some overlap at the edges, and as the market grows there will naturally be some competition. That's healthy. But inference demand is growing so quickly that this isn't a zero-sum game right now. The bigger challenge for all of us is that models keep getting larger, workloads keep getting more complex, and compute is still expensive. If we keep pushing the efficiency frontier and keep the community strong, I think we'll be in a good position no matter how the landscape shifts.

r001.rationale: The response says there is overlap and some competition, but does not say Baseten or Fireworks may view Ying Sheng’s company as a competitor.

r002.rationale: It links open-source engines to a shared ecosystem, but does not clearly connect the company’s open-source commitment to a desire to treat Baseten and Fireworks as allies.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think about it as a zero-sum thing right now, and part of that is just the position we're in. Baseten and Fireworks are both heavy users of SGLang. They've contributed back to the project, their engineers are in our Slack, and some of the performance work they've done on their side has ended up improving the open source engine for everyone. So day to day, they feel much more like partners and collaborators than competitors.

That said, I'm not naive about it. We are all sitting in the inference layer, and the inference layer is getting crowded. If you squint, anyone who serves open models at scale is a potential competitor to anyone else doing it. The question is really what you're actually selling. Fireworks and Baseten are, to me, primarily serving platforms. They sell you an endpoint, reliability, a good developer experience, and they do that very well. What we care about most is the engine itself: the kernels, the scheduler, the cache management, the stuff that decides how many tokens per second you get out of a given GPU. That's a different layer, and it's a layer where being open source is a real advantage, because the whole community is pushing on it with us.

Where it could get interesting is if they decide the engine is their differentiator and start building their own closed stack, or if we move up and start offering something that looks more like a hosted platform. Both of those are possible. But I'd rather have that be a problem of too much success than worry about it too early. The pie is growing so fast right now that the bigger risk is not keeping up with model releases and hardware changes, not losing a customer to Fireworks.

And I'll say one more thing. In this space, the companies that treat open source as a moat to protect tend to lose. The ones that treat it as a way to move faster than everyone else tend to win. So as long as we keep making SGLang the fastest and most reliable option, and as long as those teams keep finding value in building on it, I think there's plenty of room for all of us. If one day that changes, we'll compete, and I think we'd be fine.

r001.rationale: The response says they currently feel like partners and collaborators, while also calling everyone in the inference layer a potential competitor. It does not say Baseten or Fireworks may view Ying Sheng’s company as a competitor while her company does not view them that way.

r002.rationale: The response links their contributions to SGLang and the open source engine’s benefits for everyone with seeing Baseten and Fireworks as partners and collaborators.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s certainly potential for competition. We’re working in related areas, and as these companies evolve, some overlap is natural. But I wouldn’t assume that we’ll all end up building the same thing. A lot depends on which customers we focus on and which problems we choose to solve.

The way I’d approach it is to stay focused on what our customers need and where we can deliver something meaningfully better. We should pay attention to Baseten and Fireworks, but we shouldn’t let competitors define our roadmap.
